extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, university administrators, scholars of higher education, and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive standards and evaluative criteria for (a) the organization, aims, and quality of universities and colleges in the United States, and (b) principles governing the relationship between Church and State. The page lists deficiencies, recommended remedies, and constitutional/social rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional model university
rubrics_metrics.description: The development in each region of the country — in each populous State or in each group of less populous States — of at least one University which may serve as a model to the others in that section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A model institution should set before others 'the organs of activity and the excellences of arrangement and method which a first-rate place of education, learning, and research ought to possess.' Where none exist, one should be created; in some parts of the country several universities already serve as patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive faculty salaries
rubrics_metrics.description: There is required a higher scale of salaries for the teaching staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher pay is needed to attract able, learned, and inspiring teachers. The text notes this is especially acute in the United States where other careers are attractive and living costs are rising; raising salaries is presented as a practical means to improve instruction and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undergraduate intellectual life
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be a stronger pulse of intellectual life among the undergraduates in the 'College' or Academic department; students should acquire a taste for intellectual enjoyment rather than being chiefly absorbed by athletics and social amusements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal is undergraduates keenly interested in their studies and the 'things of the mind.' Antipatterns include widespread preoccupation with athletic contests (e.g., football) and social life that leave only minimal effort to obtain a degree. Remedies implied include honour courses and competitions for literary and scientific distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and realization of general liberal education
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception of a general liberal education — educating men 'for life as a whole' over and above training for a particular profession — must be sufficiently valued and effectively realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberal subjects (literature, philosophy, history, natural science) should be taught in a broad and stimulating way to implant 'largeness of view and philosophic habit of thought.' Antipattern: excessive pressure of practical subjects and treating liberal learning as secondary to professional training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid proliferation of weak colleges
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid planting several weak colleges where one strong one would better serve the region; the wasteful multiplication of mediocre institutions lowers overall standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes uncoordinated growth that produces many mediocre colleges, leading to wastage of effort and money and a general lowering of the conception of what a university ought to be. Systematic direction (not uniformity) is recommended to prevent this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain high entrance requirements and degree standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Weakness has meant acquiescence in a low standard of entrance requirements and in degrees which witness to no high level of attainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially in newer States where secondary schooling is still developing, low entry standards have permitted superficiality. Raising entrance standards and ensuring degrees represent substantial attainment are presented as central to quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in instructional quality and faculty, not only material improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: While enlarging buildings, libraries, scientific apparatus, and gymnasia is visible and easy, the slower and more difficult task is to secure more able, more learned, more inspiring teachers and to improve instruction and the standard of attainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material improvements impress visitors, but genuine quality gain requires hiring better teachers and improving methods. The natural tendency is upward as institutions emulate exemplary places; emphasis should be on instructional excellence rather than only on infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: High professional-school standards (especially medicine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintenance of a high level in professional schools, notably medicine, is essential for public safety; there are too many weak medical schools and the imperative is for fewer and better ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Carnegie Foundation (1909) is cited: the country has more medical schools than all Europe, many producing poorly trained physicians. The recommended remedy is consolidation and raising standards so professional training does not endanger the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: University mission: devotion to Truth and independence from wealth/politics
rubrics_metrics.description: The mission of a University is to 'seek and find and set forth the real values' and many teachers 'feel that the first object of their devotion is Truth.' Universities generally are not governed by considerations of size or money and should avoid deleterious contact with politics or capitalist groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should prioritize truth and intellectual values over being dazzled by wealth; independence from politics and economic pressures preserves dignity and influence. Good alumni networks help maintain broad societal influence without political entanglement.

rubrics_metrics.name: State neutrality in religious matters (constitutional prohibitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Constitution prohibits religious tests for office and forbids laws respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting free exercise (Art. VI and the First Amendment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions mean the National government must neither establish a church nor interfere with the free exercise of religion. While these affect the federal government only, most State constitutions echo similar prohibitions; exceptions in some States are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil power should abstain from interfering in faith and worship; equality of religious bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: All religious bodies are absolutely equal before the law and unrecognized by the law, except as voluntary associations; the civil power should be neutral and impartial among different forms of faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most State constitutions declare freedom of worship and often forbid compelling support or attendance at any church. The text emphasizes widespread American acceptance that the State ought to leave religious matters alone, treating them like artistic or literary pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and exceptions to neutrality (when social harm is threatened)
rubrics_metrics.description: The political rationale for abstention holds that civil compulsion in religious matters is an infringement on liberty and equality, justifiable only when a religious practice is so obviously anti-social or immoral as to threaten community well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include prosecution of polygamy (Idaho disenfranchisements) and other practices regarded as socially harmful. The principle allows State action only to the extent necessary to prevent obvious social harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious bodies should remain autonomous and avoid State control or endowment
rubrics_metrics.description: Churches as spiritual bodies prefer to be left absolutely to themselves, not patronized by civil power, not restrained by law except when they intermeddle in secular affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State establishment or endowment would restrict a church's internal organization, discipline, and finances and expose it to jealousy from other sects. Clergy and bishops are said to prefer freedom to any State advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public funding of denominational institutions must be for secular/charitable purposes and not political patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriations to religiously-managed charitable or educational institutions may sometimes be the readiest way to promote a public purpose, but such grants must purport to be for philanthropic or educational purposes and not to purchase political support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns of antipatterns: legislatures giving money to particular denominational institutions to secure votes (cited examples in New York; Roman Catholic charities receiving large sums). Where grants are made, they should be transparently for public benefit, not sectarian favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious organizations should avoid political interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing excites more general disapprobation than any attempt by an ecclesiastical organization to interfere in politics; suspicion that a church guides members' votes can provoke anti-religious or nativist movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: anti-Catholic movements and hostility to Mormonism arose partly from fears of clerical political influence. The normative claim is that ecclesiastical bodies ought not to seek political ends or directives for their members' civic behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical-political rationale for secular abstention
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principled justifications for State abstention are presented: (a) political — liberty and equality require no State compulsion or favoritism in religion; (b) religious — the church as a spiritual body must not be subjected to State compulsion if it is to live by love and reverence rather than law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The former argument settled the question practically in early American republic days; the latter accords with religious preferences for autonomy. The text also notes American conceptions of the State as a limited administrative body rather than an ideal moral power, which reinforces abstention.
